newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian govt seeks to salvage immigrant reprieve.
newsitem.headline: Italian govt seeks to salvage immigrant reprieve.

text.p: Italy's centre-left government called a confidence vote in the Senate (upper house) on Wednesday to rush through a draft law governing the status of some 250,000 previously illegal immigrants.

Interior Minister Giorgo Napolitano said 7,000 blocking amendments, most of them from the hard-right National Alliance party, would make consideration of the draft law "impossible in the time that the absolute urgency of the matter requires".
Parliamentary party leaders in the Senate set the vote for around six p.m. (1700 GMT). It will sweep aside the amendments if the government wins.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi's coalition has a sizeable majority in the assembly and did not appear at risk of a defeat on the motion, an outcome which would bring the cabinet down.
National Alliance, which alone has submitted 6,018 amendments, called the decision to resort to a confidence vote an affront to parliament.

"It is yet another demonstration of the Soviet-style arrogance of the Prodi government, which is preventing the opposition from carrying out its constitutional role," senior National Alliance politician Maurizio Gasparri said.
Thousands of immigrants, many from Africa, Albania and the Philippines, enter Italy without visas or work papers, many on small boats from across the Adriatic or from North Africa.

They were given a chance to regularise their status under a partial amnesty last November, when the then government issued a decree allowing illegal immigrants already in the country to remain as long as they registered with police.

The stop-gap legislation, never converted into law, has been re-issued five times but cannot be rolled over again. The vacuum has raised doubts about whether foreigners who took advantage of the measures are now safe from possible expulsion.
Cesare Salvi, leader in the Senate of the main force in govenment, the Democratic Party of the Left, said failure to end the uncertainty would dent Italy's international credibility.
"There are 250,000 foreign workers who have put their trust in commitments assumed by Italy and have come out into the open to ask for their status to be regularised," Salvi said.
The Constitutional Court last month banned the practice by which successive governments have re-issued decrees, which lapse after 60 days unless they are passed into law by parliament.
The ruling has forced Prodi's government to put several decrees to confidence votes to rush them into law or to replace them by draft laws.

Napolitano told the Senate that the immigration law applied only to foreigners who had legalised their position under the old decrees. He said it would not prejudice consideration by parliament of longer-term regulations on immigration.
National Alliance, part of the main centre-right Freedom Alliance opposition bloc, has long argued that all illegal immigrants should be expelled.
